LinkedIn's profile now impacts your post ranking.

Your headline, About section, and featured content are algorithm signals. 
A vague headline buries your posts even if the content is good.

The difference between 2-3% engagement and 6%+ comes down to what you're tracking. 
One approach watches saves and dwell time while the other measures likes and impressions.

When someone saves your post, they're bookmarking it to use later. 
When they spend 60 seconds on your post instead of 3, the algorithm treats it completely differently.

Consistency matters more than volume while posting on LinkedIn. 
Posting at the same time every week and replying to comments creates more momentum that posting 10 times one week can't match.

Start tracking these metrics. 
Within weeks, you'll see patterns in what actually works for your audience.

items.content:
I recorded 6 months of my sales calls with an AI.
Here is what the data showed me.

My real pitch only starts ten or fifteen minutes into the call.
The first part is a conversation about them, where they are now, what they use day to day, what works, what is broken, and whether they are happy with what they pay for it.

While they answer all of that, they hand me their objections without knowing it.

Four of them come back on almost every call.
When I pull up the deals that closed, these are the answers I gave.
I am not saying the words closed the deal.
The data just keeps pointing at the same ones.

→ "We already have tools for this."
↳ I never trash the tool they already use.
I ask what works for them, and the one thing they would change about it.
That one thing is usually where I fit.

→ "We handle it in house."
↳ I make it clear I am not there to replace their team.
Then I ask what doing it themselves takes, in hours and people, and I show them where I make it lighter.

→ "It's not a priority right now."
↳ This tells me I have not made the problem feel urgent enough.
I ask what would have to change for it to move up the list, and what another quarter of waiting costs them.
If the honest answer is nothing, I let it go.

→ "We don't have the budget."
↳ When someone says this, I stop talking about price.
I go back to what the problem is already costing them every month, because that is almost always the real conversation.

None of this shows up one call at a time.
I keep Claap running on every call.
It records, syncs to my CRM, and lets me pull up the closed deals and see which responses keep showing up in my best months.

I even built an objection dashboard straight from my calls, no code needed.
Here is how I set it up, if you want your own:
https://lnkd.in/d5zKXAZk

BONUS:
ANTI SALES is the most honest thing I do, and it wins me the most deals.
When I am clearly not the right fit (too expensive for what they need), I say it straight and point them to a competitor who fits better.
Those are the people who come back, or refer me.

items.content:
Your best posts won't matter if your profile doesn't convert.

People spend 6-10 seconds scanning your profile to decide whether to message you or move on. 
If your current profile converts 1% of visitors into conversations and an optimized profile moves that to 3%, every 100 profile views matters. 

Optimized LinkedIn profiles are more likely to appear in search results and help convert profile visitors into leads. 

Here are 5 prompts to audit your LinkedIn profile in 5 minutes-

Headline Optimization Prompt: 
"My LinkedIn headline is: [INSERT YOUR HEADLINE] | I help: [INSERT WHO YOU HELP] | The problem I solve: [INSERT THE PROBLEM] | Keywords people search for in my industry: [INSERT 3-5 KEYWORDS] Audit this headline on 3 things: 1. Is it clear what I do? 2. Does it mention who I help? 3. Does it include searchable keywords? If weak, rewrite it better."

About Section Prompt: 
"This is my LinkedIn About section: [PASTE YOUR FULL ABOUT TEXT] | The problem I solve: [INSERT PROBLEM] | My ideal customer: [INSERT WHO THEY ARE] Rate this About section on: 1. Does the first two sentences make clear what problem I solve? 2. Would my ideal customer see themselves in this? 3. Is there a clear CTA (link, contact, next step)? Rewrite the weak parts."

Experience Description Prompt: 
"Here are my LinkedIn experience descriptions: [PASTE EACH JOB DESCRIPTION] For each role, tell me if it shows what I accomplished and the impact or if it just lists duties. Then rewrite 2-3 descriptions to emphasize: Money saved or made, People managed, Problems solved & Business results. Not task lists."

Call to Action Prompt: 
"What I do: [INSERT WHAT YOU OFFER] | Who I help: [INSERT YOUR IDEAL CUSTOMER] | What I want them to do: [INSERT NEXT STEP - book call, DM, visit site, etc] Write me three different CTAs: 1. One for my headline 2. One for my About section 3. One for my pinned post Make them specific and action-oriented."

Featured Content Prompt: 
"What I'm currently featuring on my profile: [DESCRIBE WHAT'S PINNED] | My positioning: [INSERT WHAT YOU WANT TO BE KNOWN FOR] | My niche: [INSERT YOUR NICHE] Is my featured content proving I'm an expert in [YOUR NICHE]? If not, what 3-5 posts should I feature instead to show: Expertise in [your niche], Proof of results, Authority in [specific area]"

Copy these five and run them in Claude. You'll know exactly what to fix.

items.content:
Using one AI tool for everything limits what you get.

Know what each tool is weak at, and you'll know which one to use.

- Claude: Catches its own errors better than others (26.4% vs 36.2% confidence-contradiction rate). Use it when being wrong costs you.

- ChatGPT: Strongest for everyday productivity, creative writing, and general tasks across the board. 

- Perplexity: Leads on citation accuracy by 37%—every answer comes with sources you can actually verify. 

- Grok: Built for real-time social conversations and fast-paced interactions, especially on X for catching emerging trends. 

- Notion: Built directly into your workflows. Use it when you're already inside Notion for notes and tasks.

- NotebookLM: Everything comes cited. Use it for learning and studying because sources matter.

The Claude-Perplexity pair is structurally complementary; use them together for research that needs both precision and verification. 

Pick based on what the task actually needs. That's it

items.content:
The tool you pick determines how fast you finish a task.

Half of the slowness comes from fighting the wrong tool. 
Once you stop doing that, everything becomes much faster.

Here's how I use them:

1. Comments backing up
I use Wispr Flow to comment faster. I finish in half the time instead of typing each one out.

2. Need visuals in 10 minutes
I send ChatGPT my previous posts and my visual style as reference. 
Type it what the new post needs and then I drop it into Canva and edit the infographic. 

3. Planning a month ahead
Claude breaks down the content pillars and themes. 
Then Notion holds the calendar and I use Notion AI to organize batches.

4. Find what's trending in my niche
I go to subreddits in my space. Filter by top this month or this year and that tells me what people actually care about. 
Grok also catches conversations early before they blow up everywhere.

5. Turn one video into five posts
One YouTube video becomes five different LinkedIn posts. 
NotebookLM pulls the key points, and Notion organizes them by angle. 

6. Writing posts
I use Wispr Flow to give me a rough voice draft of what I want to say. 
I paste that into Claude and it adapts it to my actual voice and makes it sharper. One back-and-forth and it's ready.

7. Sanity check claims
I use Perplexity to fact-check before posting. 
It pulls sources so I'm not guessing if something is true.

8. Visual inspiration
I reference what works visually on Pinterest and Reddit. 
See what resonates in design, color, layout and apply those elements to my own work.

Start doing this with one task. 
You'll notice the difference immediately.

📦 Packaging Is Not a Cost. It Is Risk Management-
Many furniture manufacturers focus heavily on product quality, finishing, construction, and production efficiency.
Yet one critical factor is often underestimated:
Packaging.
A product may leave the factory in perfect condition, but its real journey starts after loading.
It will be lifted, stacked, transported, unloaded, warehoused, and finally delivered to the customer.
When packaging is properly engineered:
✅ Transit damage is reduced
✅ Customer complaints decrease
✅ Replacement costs are minimized
✅ Brand reputation is protected
✅ Customer satisfaction improves
✅ Buyer confidence increases
However, when packaging is weak or poorly designed:
❌ Product damage increases
❌ Claims and replacements rise
❌ Logistics costs increase
❌ Customer trust is affected
❌ Supplier credibility suffers
❌ Future business opportunities may be lost
The true purpose of packaging is not to pack a product.
Its purpose is to ensure that the customer receives the product exactly as the manufacturer intended.
In furniture manufacturing, packaging should be developed with the same attention as the product itself.
Because a product is only successful when it reaches the customer safely.
#Packaging #FurnitureIndustry #QualityAssurance #ProductDevelopment #ISTA #SupplyChain #FurnitureManufacturing

items.content:
Not every challenge in life can be fought.
Not every situation can be avoided.
Some problems require something smarter — strategy.
I recently watched a short wildlife clip that left me thinking.
A wild animal had a cheetah sitting on its back, ready to attack.
Running away? Not possible.
Fighting back? Almost certain death.
Instead of reacting in panic, the animal did something surprising.
It slowly walked into a nearby pond.
But the pond had crocodiles.
The moment the cheetah realized the danger, it jumped off.
Within seconds, the crocodiles turned their attention to the cheetah…
and the animal calmly walked away to safety.
No fight.
No panic.
Just smart thinking.
The lesson?
In life and in business, strategy often wins over struggle.
In corporate life, many of us carry our own “cheetah” on our backs:
• Office politics from a colleague
• A project that constantly creates pressure
• A manager who blocks new ideas
• A client who delays payments endlessly
Most people respond the same way.
They work harder.
They argue more.
They complain louder.
Yet nothing really improves.
Because sometimes the issue is not effort — it’s the approach.
Smart professionals understand this.
They don’t try to fight every battle.
They redesign the situation.
They adjust the process.
They change the conversation.
They involve the right stakeholders.
And suddenly, the problem resolves itself.
In corporate life, strength helps.
But strategy changes the game.

The non-AI skill I'm investing the most time in right now: nervous system regulation.

Hear me out, even if you think you're already pretty calm under pressure.

The more work you hand off to AI, the more you're left with the hard stuff. The ambiguous calls. The high-stakes decisions. The projects with ten open threads and no clear answer.

AI takes your easy work. What remains is harder, more complex, and more mentally taxing than what most of us are used to carrying.

That's not a complaint. It's just the math.

Which means the ability to stay clear-headed under that kind of cognitive load, to not get frazzled when things are messy and unresolved, is becoming a serious professional edge.

I'm not talking about meditation as a wellness habit. I'm talking about nervous system regulation as a performance skill. The same way you'd train for endurance if your job suddenly got more physically demanding.

The job got more demanding. Most of us haven't trained for it yet.

Curious if anyone else is thinking about this. What non-technical skills are you investing in right now as AI changes the shape of your work?

items.content:
Fable is Anthropic's most powerful AI model (and also most expensive). Here's how to get it to train cheaper AI models and save $$

Not because the expensive model isn't worth it. But because they're using it wrong.

Here's the framework AI companies use internally, called model distillation, and how you can apply it yourself.

What AI labs do:
They train an expensive model on a specific task until it's really good at that task. Then they use that expensive model to generate the data for a cheaper model needs to do the same job.

Expensive model builds the playbook. Cheap model runs it.

You can do the exact same thing.

When I'm building a new AI workflow, I always start with the most capable model I have access to. I use it to develop and refine the playbook for that process. I have it critique the playbook. Update it. Run it. Improve it.

Once the playbook is solid, I test it on a cheaper model.

Nine times out of ten, a well-written playbook runs just fine on a cheaper model. The expensive model did the hard thinking. The cheap model executes.

You keep the expensive model in your back pocket for genuinely novel problems. But your day-to-day workflows? Those can run cheap.

So if you're experimenting with Fable right now, use it to build the playbook. Not just to run tasks.

The goal isn't to use the most powerful model for everything. The goal is to use it once, well, so everything else gets cheaper.

items.content:
Most people let their AI infer context about them randomly. I actually tell mine exactly what to know.

I call it a personal README. And it's one of the highest-leverage things I've done to get better AI output.

Here are the 6 things I include:

1. Who I am
Basic background. Not a bio, just enough context to ground everything else.

2. How I think
Do I make fast decisions or deliberate ones? Do I optimize for simplicity or first principles? Do I care more about reducing risk or moving fast? This one changes how the AI frames every piece of advice it gives me.

3. My actual work
The types of tasks, responsibilities, and domains I operate in. Without this, AI defaults to generic. With it, everything becomes specific.

4. How I work with others
How I want to show up in different situations. Meetings, feedback, leadership moments. Useful any time I'm asking for help navigating a people situation.

5. Mental models, frameworks, and mentors I admire
This is where it gets interesting. When AI knows which thinkers and frameworks I already trust, its advice actually fits my worldview instead of contradicting it.

6. A glossary of key terms
Every industry and every person has their own language. I define mine so I stop repeating myself and the AI stops misinterpreting me.

The last two have given me the most leverage by far.

If you're using AI heavily in your work and you haven't built something like this, you're essentially starting from scratch every single conversation.

Curious if anyone else has done something similar. What would you add to the list?

items.content:
Everyone says 'give your AI more context' but nobody shows you what that actually means.

Here's the specific thing I do.

Before I start any AI task, I ask myself: if I asked the AI a question about the background information I assume it knows, would it get it right?

If I'm not sure, I just ask it directly.

For example: 'List out our current products, what they cost, and who they're targeted to.'

That's it. One simple prompt reveals exactly what your AI knows and what it doesn't.

Maybe it has the right products but outdated pricing. Maybe it has no idea what that internal acronym means. Maybe it's working with information from six months ago.

You won't know until you check.

This takes 30 seconds and saves you from generating outputs that are confidently wrong about your own business.

AI doesn't tell you what it doesn't know. So you have to ask.

Test your context before you assume it's there.

items.content:
I turned off built-in memory in most of my AI accounts. 

Not because memory is bad.

Because memory makes AI feel smarter... but not always more reliable (!!)

Example:
- Today Claude was running my email triage playbook.
- I had sent over a team member’s calendar booking link for an edge case email.
- Then Claude remembered it.
- And decided it should start sending THAT link instead of mine.

Luckily I caught it.

But this is exactly the problem with built-in memory in operational workflows.

It can take a one-off exception and quietly turn it into a new rule.

Which is terrifying if you’re using AI for actual business processes.

For brainstorming? Great.

For personalization? Maybe useful.

For production workflows?
I want the AI following the playbook... not guessing what I “probably” want based on something it saw yesterday.

The source of truth should be the playbooks, not the AI tool's memory.

This is one of those AI ops lessons that feels small until it breaks something.

Memory can make AI feel more human. But in operations, I don’t want more human.

I want more reliable.
